title: Gerstmann syndrome: dominant angular gyrus (parietal association cortex)
vignette: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to an acute change in mental status. The patient was having dinner with his family when he suddenly had difficulty using his fork and appeared confused. Other medical conditions include type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension. The patient is a high school calculus teacher and has a 40-pack-year smoking history. Blood pressure is 180/98 mm Hg and pulse is 98/min and regular. On physical examination, the patient is well oriented, answers questions appropriately, and has no motor, sensory, or visual deficits. He is unable to add simple numbers such as 17 plus 9; he is also unable to recognize or distinguish his fingers. A lateral view of the brain with several labeled regions (A-E) is shown. Which of the following labeled brain areas is most likely affected in this patient?

clues.note: Hypertension (180/98) plus diabetes/smoking are vascular risk factors for the acute ischemic stroke that produced this focal cortical syndrome.

clues.text: no motor, sensory, or visual deficits
clues.note: Deficits of higher-order integration WITHOUT motor/sensory/visual loss point to the parietal ASSOCIATION cortex (angular gyrus), not primary cortices.

clues.text: unable to add simple numbers such as 17 plus 9
clues.note: Acalculia (loss of calculation) despite being a calculus teacher is a core sign of Gerstmann syndrome, localizing to the dominant angular gyrus.

clues.text: unable to recognize or distinguish his fingers
clues.note: Finger agnosia (inability to identify one's own fingers) is another Gerstmann-syndrome sign of dominant angular gyrus injury.

whatMatters: Acalculia + finger agnosia (with intact motor/sensory/vision) = Gerstmann syndrome from a stroke of the DOMINANT (usually left) ANGULAR GYRUS of the parietal association cortex. On the diagram this is the parietal lobe region posterior to the somatosensory cortex - label D. Answer D.
strategy: Recognize the Gerstmann tetrad (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation) -> dominant angular gyrus (inferior parietal lobule). On the labeled brain, pick the parietal-association region (D), not the precentral motor gyrus (A), postcentral sensory gyrus (B), Broca area (C), or occipital visual cortex (E).

options.text: Region A (precentral gyrus / primary motor cortex)
Region B (postcentral gyrus / primary somatosensory cortex)
Region C (Broca area, inferior frontal gyrus)
Region D (angular gyrus, inferior parietal lobule)

eliminations.label: Region A - primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex), just anterior to the central sulcus. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a lesion here causes contralateral weakness, but this patient has NO motor deficit. ✅ Correct if: contralateral hemiparesis in a somatotopic (homunculus) pattern.

eliminations.label: Region B - primary somatosensory cortex (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex), just posterior to the central sulcus. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a lesion causes contralateral sensory loss, but this patient's sensation is intact and his deficits are higher-order integrative (calculation, finger identification). ✅ Correct if: contralateral loss of touch/proprioception.

eliminations.label: Region C - Broca area (expressive aphasia)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area) of the dominant hemisphere. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a lesion causes non-fluent (expressive) aphasia, but this patient speaks and answers appropriately. ✅ Correct if: effortful, non-fluent speech with intact comprehension.

eliminations.label: Region E - primary visual cortex (occipital)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the occipital primary visual cortex. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a lesion causes contralateral visual field loss/cortical blindness, but this patient has no visual deficit. ✅ Correct if: homonymous hemianopia/cortical visual loss.

reasoning: Acalculia + finger agnosia with intact motor/sensory/vision = higher-order parietal association deficit
This is Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation)
Gerstmann syndrome localizes to the dominant (left) angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule
mechanism: The parietal ASSOCIATION cortex integrates multisensory (visual-spatial, tactile, proprioceptive) information to support comprehension and problem-solving. The angular gyrus of the DOMINANT (usually left) inferior parietal lobule is critical for language-related symbolic processing; a focal lesion here (commonly an ischemic stroke, given this patient's hypertension, diabetes, and smoking) classically produces GERSTMANN SYNDROME: agraphia (impaired writing), acalculia (impaired calculation), finger agnosia (inability to identify fingers), and left-right disorientation - all WITHOUT primary motor, sensory, or visual loss, because the primary cortices are spared. On a lateral brain map, the angular gyrus lies in the parietal lobe posterior to the postcentral (somatosensory) gyrus and above the occipital lobe (label D). The distractors are primary/other functional areas: precentral motor (A -> contralateral weakness), postcentral sensory (B -> contralateral sensory loss), Broca (C -> expressive aphasia), and occipital visual cortex (E -> visual field loss).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Neuro > Gerstmann syndrome (dominant angular gyrus): agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation; parietal association cortex; cortical localization map.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Higher-order deficits (calculation, finger ID) with intact primary functions localize to the parietal association cortex/angular gyrus.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on Gerstmann syndrome, angular gyrus, agraphia/acalculia/finger agnosia, or association vs primary cortex? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Primary motor (A)/sensory (B)/visual (E) lesions cause deficits this patient lacks; Broca (C) causes aphasia, but he speaks normally.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: On the lateral brain diagram: A/B flank the central sulcus (A precentral motor, B postcentral sensory), C is Broca in the inferior frontal gyrus, D is the parietal angular gyrus, E is occipital visual cortex. Anchor: 'acalculia + finger agnosia = angular gyrus = D.'

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: Gerstmann = agraphia + acalculia + finger agnosia + left-right disorientation -> dominant angular gyrus.
